title: Universal neural network approximation of symmetric polyconvex energies and envelopes
authors: Florian Gammer
abstract: Symmetric polyconvexity provides a sufficient condition for weak lower semicontinuity in small-strain elasticity and a tractable lower bound for the relaxation of non-(quasi)convex energies. Since classical algorithms for computing such functions can be computationally expensive, neural network approximations have recently emerged as an alternative. A central difficulty with establishing such neural network based approaches for symmetric polyconvexity is the additional monotonicity property. As we show, the corresponding weight restrictions on ReLU-based input-convex networks do not yield universal approximation of the lifted representers. Here, we introduce symmetric polyconvex neural networks (SPCNNs) for constitutive modeling and approximation of symmetric polyconvex envelopes. The deep architecture combines convexity with the monotonicity required of a representer in the space of minors. We prove a universal approximation theorem for symmetric polyconvex energies, without requiring isotropy, and quantify the number of affine pieces attainable by the lifted network and derive reduced architectures for isotropic energies. Numerical examples illustrate stress-based regression and approximation of the symmetric polyconvex envelope of a double-well potential. Symmetric polyconvexity is guaranteed by construction, while the accuracy of the fitted energies and envelopes is assessed numerically.

infographic.key_insight: Symmetric polyconvex neural networks (SPCNNs) guarantee symmetric polyconvexity by construction and universally approximate symmetric polyconvex energies without assuming isotropy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: SPCNNs provide a structure-preserving approach to small-strain constitutive modeling and approximation of lower bounds for relaxed nonconvex energies.
method: Combine convexity with the required monotonicity in a lifted space of minors.
Prove universal approximation and quantify the lifted network’s attainable affine pieces.
Derive reduced architectures for isotropic energies.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical examples demonstrate stress-based regression and approximation of the symmetric polyconvex envelope of a double-well potential.
infographic.watch_item: Symmetric polyconvexity is guaranteed, but fitted accuracy is assessed numerically; an envelope approximation should not be equated with the exact relaxed energy.
infographic.paper_title: Universal neural network approximation of symmetric polyconvex energies and envelopes

title: Microstructural Generative Inverse Models for Additive Manufacturing Digital Twins
authors: Pablo Luna Falcon, Jason Mayeur, Amirkoushyar Ziabari, Vincent Paquit, Patxi Fernandez-Zelaia
abstract: Metal additive manufacturing (AM) offers substantial advantages to the fabrication of complex structural components, but its widespread adoption is slowed due to complexities in the process-structure-property relations which is the cause for uncertainty and drives risk. Accurately quantifying these complex relations solely via experimental workflows is time consuming and costly. Integrated computational materials and engineering (ICME) frameworks address this challenge by leveraging advanced computational tools, such as crystal plasticity finite element models (CPFEM), to predict critical mechanical properties directly from microstructural data. However, these frameworks require a large datasets that are often difficult to obtain, and their predictive accuracy depends on the availability of realistic AM microstructure representations. Generative deep learning models are a promising approach towards synthesizing AM microstructures which contain complex morphological and crystallographic features. Denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs), in particular, show a strong potential to capture the inherent complexities of AM structures. In this work, we demonstrate that DDPMs can reliably synthesize digital-twin orientation-imaging micrographs, and we support this claim with quantitative evidence of the fidelity of the generated samples. Additionally, we establish a classifier-free guidance framework for solving complex inverse problems such as property-to-structure and process-to-structure mappings, and we showcase a potential application on a qualification-relevant uncertainty quantification problem. Our work highlights the potential of AI-based generative modeling as a key component of computational frameworks for accelerating AM materials qualification and certification.

infographic.key_insight: Denoising diffusion models generate realistic additive-manufacturing orientation micrographs and enable inverse mappings from properties or process conditions to microstructure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Synthetic microstructures could support CPFEM-based digital twins and uncertainty quantification, helping accelerate metal AM qualification.
method: Train denoising diffusion probabilistic models to synthesize orientation-imaging micrographs.
Use classifier-free guidance for property-to-structure and process-to-structure inverse problems.
Demonstrate a qualification-relevant uncertainty quantification application.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports quantitative evidence of generated-sample fidelity but does not specify dataset sizes, evaluation metrics, or numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Micrograph fidelity alone does not establish accurate downstream mechanical predictions or generalization across AM conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Microstructural Generative Inverse Models for Additive Manufacturing Digital Twins

title: Scalable Stress-Constrained Topology Optimization: A Super-resolution and Simultaneous Approach Based on Machine Learning
authors: Xiangyu Sun, Shirin Hosseinmardi, Ramin Bostanabad
abstract: Large-scale topology optimization (TO) remains computationally demanding, especially for stress-constrained problems. To address this challenge, we propose the simultaneous neural topology optimization (SNTO) framework where we represent state, adjoint, and design variables with custom neural networks (NNs) whose parameters are jointly optimized within a single optimization loop that leverages continuous adjoint analysis and automatic differentiation. This optimization minimizes a multi-component loss function that combines the design objective, an aggregation of the local stress constraints, and the potential energy functionals. Our NNs have a unique architecture that accelerates convergence while enabling the networks to capture sharp gradients and boundaries which are critical to stress-constrained TO. To achieve scalability to millions of degrees of freedom (DoF), we develop a hardware-aware training scheme in which the design domain is partitioned into subdomains that are distributed across multiple GPUs. To control peak GPU memory usage, we further slice each subdomain into smaller regions whose loss gradients are evaluated sequentially and accumulated to update the NN parameters. Unlike domain decomposition approaches, our partitioning naturally ensures field continuity across the subdomains and does not require the introduction of additional terms into the loss function. For validation, we first evaluate the proposed framework on various 2D stress-constrained benchmarks and compare our results to a conventional finite element-based approach, showing that SNTO produces super-resolution designs with sharper boundaries, smaller gray areas, and lower volume fractions. We then consider large-scale 3D problems with up to eight million collocation points and distribute the training over up to eight GPUs.

infographic.key_insight: Simultaneous neural topology optimization jointly learns state, adjoint, and design fields to produce super-resolution stress-constrained designs at large scales.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework targets computational bottlenecks in designing material-efficient structures subject to local stress limits.
method: Jointly optimize custom neural networks using continuous adjoint analysis and automatic differentiation.
Combine the design objective, aggregated local stress constraints, and potential energy functionals in one loss.
Distribute spatial partitions across GPUs and accumulate gradients over smaller slices to control peak memory while preserving field continuity.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports sharper boundaries, smaller gray areas, and lower volume fractions than a conventional FEM-based approach on 2D benchmarks, plus 3D demonstrations with up to eight million collocation points and eight GPUs.
infographic.watch_item: Aggregated stress constraints and neural field approximations warrant independent checks of local peak stresses and constraint satisfaction.
infographic.paper_title: Scalable Stress-Constrained Topology Optimization: A Super-resolution and Simultaneous Approach Based on Machine Learning

title: Synthetic Dataset Generation, Physical Consistency and Active Learning for Shape-Informed Surrogate Modeling of Hemodynamics
authors: Francesco Romor, Richard Schussnig, Charles A. Taylor, Gerhard A. Holzapfel, Alfonso Caiazzo
abstract: Model order reduction has the potential to enable real-time patient-specific assessment of cardiovascular flows. However, it still faces significant challenges stemming from the geometric variability of vascular anatomies. Building upon the SynthAorta dataset (Bosnjak et al., IEEE Trans. Med. Imag. 45(1), 2026) of physiological aortic geometries, we generate an extensive dataset of physiologically consistent computational fluid dynamics solutions through an automatic boundary-condition adjustment procedure. A common reference geometry allows all patient-specific anatomies to be represented by displacement fields, providing point-to-point correspondence without the need for geometric registration. Based on this dataset, we develop Graph U-Net and Transformer U-Net surrogate models to predict velocity and pressure fields at peak systole. We further investigate two strategies to enhance data efficiency and prediction accuracy: active learning and differentiable physical consistency constraints based on the finite element residual. The results show that active learning is strongly regime-dependent: while it offers little benefit over random sampling during early training, it improves performance during fine-tuning through gradient- and subspace-based acquisition strategies. Similarly, physical consistency constraints prove to be substantially more effective as a fine-tuning objective than as a regularizer applied throughout training. Finally, out-of-distribution studies demonstrate that the primary limitation of surrogate models lies in the geometric support of the underlying parametrization rather than in the neural network architectures themselves. The proposed framework combines synthetic dataset generation, geometry-aware surrogate modeling, physics-informed optimization, and active learning into a scalable workflow for inter-patient hemodynamic prediction.

infographic.key_insight: For shape-informed hemodynamic surrogates, active learning and finite-element physical consistency are more effective during fine-tuning than during early or full-course training.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The workflow supports scalable prediction of patient-specific aortic velocity and pressure fields, advancing the goal of real-time cardiovascular flow assessment.
method: Generate physiologically consistent CFD data from SynthAorta geometries using automatic boundary-condition adjustment.
Represent anatomy through displacement fields on a common reference geometry and train Graph U-Net and Transformer U-Net surrogates.
Improve predictions through active learning and differentiable finite-element residual constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: Peak-systolic velocity and pressure evaluations show fine-tuning benefits from gradient- and subspace-based acquisition, while out-of-distribution tests identify geometric coverage as the main limitation.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization remains constrained by the geometric support of the anatomy parametrization; architectural changes alone may not overcome this limitation.
infographic.paper_title: Synthetic Dataset Generation, Physical Consistency and Active Learning for Shape-Informed Surrogate Modeling of Hemodynamics

title: Multi-Material Topology Optimization of Phononic Crystals for Targeted Elastic Wave Bandgap
authors: Bir Bahadur Chaudhary, Wenfeng Li, Ting Chen, Xinmai Yang, Candan Tamerler, Bin Ouyang
abstract: Phononic crystals are periodic elastic structures that exhibit frequency bandgaps within which elastic waves cannot propagate. The formation and width of these bandgaps depend on the spatial distribution of material properties within periodic phononic unit cells. In this work, we propose novel topology optimization formulations to achieve multi-material design of phononic crystals for bandgap optimization at targeted frequencies, where we discover the influence of spatially varying properties of base materials on the band structures that block and permit elastic wave propagation. Specifically, we model wave propagation by Floquet-Bloch theory and solve the resulting eigenvalue problem by the finite element method along the boundary of the irreducible Brillouin zone. We first propose a multivariate weight-based method via a novel interpolation scheme that maps the design variables of an arbitrary number of candidate materials into effective density and stiffness for elastic wave-propagation calculations, where bandgaps arise from the contrast in the stiffness and inertia among material constituents. We then develop two formulations for bandgap optimization. The first formulation maximizes the gap between two adjacent frequency bands using a bound-based approach, where we introduce two auxiliary scalar variables as additional design variables and incorporate them directly into the design objective, yielding a linear, differentiable design objective, with the eigenfrequencies entering the formulation through associated constraints. The second formulation places a bandgap over a user-defined target frequency range through a dynamic band-pairing strategy, where we adaptively identify the relevant pair of adjacent bands amid optimization iterations. Towards the end, we validate the bandgap performance of our designs against the transmission loss spectra computed from COMSOL Multiphysics.

infographic.key_insight: Multi-material topology optimization designs phononic crystals with widened elastic-wave bandgaps or bandgaps aligned to a user-defined frequency range.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports frequency-selective vibration isolation and elastic-wave filtering through engineered periodic material layouts.
method: Compute dispersion bands using Floquet–Bloch theory and finite-element eigenvalue analysis along the irreducible Brillouin-zone boundary.
Interpolate effective density and stiffness from design weights for multiple candidate materials.
Optimize adjacent-band separation with auxiliary bounds, or target a frequency range using adaptive band pairing.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports validation of optimized bandgap performance against transmission-loss spectra computed in COMSOL Multiphysics, but provides no quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Repeated finite-element eigenvalue solves may be computationally costly; no learned surrogate or experimental validation is described in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Multi-Material Topology Optimization of Phononic Crystals for Targeted Elastic Wave Bandgap

title: Robust topology optimization of isogeometric Kirchhoff--Love shells by the Speed Method
authors: Philipp Eisenhardt, Fernando Hübner Scherer, Barbara Wohlmuth, Andrei Constantinescu
abstract: This paper presents a framework for robust topology optimization of Kirchhoff-Love (KL) multi-patch shells using isogeometric analysis and non-matching meshes and provides a CAD-compatible method. The material distribution is optimized via a NURBS-based level set method, enabling accurate boundary representation and seamless export to standard CAD/CAM workflows. The shape derivative is computed using the speed method, yielding a volume-based formulation that avoids boundary approximations and aligns with the isogeometric principle of coarse, high-order discretizations. This eliminates the need for local refinement, adaptive quadrature, or trimming as the descent direction for the compliance and volume objectives are obtained through a biharmonic equation. The framework is extended to robust optimization under uncertainty, accounting for stochastic loading and material properties via Monte Carlo sampling and Gaussian Random Fields. Numerical examples demonstrate the method's efficiency and robustness across single- and multi-patch shells, reproducing literature results with fewer elements than traditional FEM or refined IGA approaches. The developed methods and tools can be directly extended to problems involving stress-based optimization and risk-averse metrics. The numerical implementations are open-source and available on GitHub.

infographic.key_insight: A NURBS-based level set framework enables robust, CAD-compatible topology optimization of Kirchhoff–Love shells using volume-based shape derivatives from the speed method.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports lightweight shell design under uncertain loads and material properties while preserving compatibility with CAD/CAM workflows.
method: Use isogeometric analysis for multi-patch shells with non-matching meshes.
Compute volume-based shape derivatives and biharmonic descent directions without local refinement, adaptive quadrature, or trimming.
Represent uncertainty with Monte Carlo sampling and Gaussian random fields.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical single- and multi-patch examples reproduce literature results with fewer elements than traditional FEM or refined isogeometric approaches, according to the abstract.
infographic.watch_item: Monte Carlo sampling may increase optimization cost; the abstract does not quantify runtime savings or sampling convergence.
infographic.paper_title: Robust topology optimization of isogeometric Kirchhoff--Love shells by the Speed Method

title: Nested Sparsity for Scalable Pretraining and Continual Learning
authors: Tianzhe Chu, Druv Pai, Yi Ma
abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) transformers, the standard backbone for modern large-scale deep learning, employ conditional computation: only a sparse subset of model weights is used in each forward pass. In MoE transformers, this sparsity arises in the MoE operator, which generalizes the multi-layer perceptron in the classical transformer. In this work, we explore an alternative mechanism for conditional computation that analogously generalizes the attention operator. The sparsity induced by this mechanism naturally nests (i.e., hierarchically composes) with the sparsity induced by the MoE operator. We show that a transformer employing this nested sparsity mechanism, which we call Nestor, performs better than a conventional MoE transformer at equal compute and equal sparsity in language model pretraining. We also show that Nestor is well-suited for continual pretraining: it can be adapted to longer contexts more effectively than conventional MoEs, as well as adapt more efficiently to new domains while forgetting less on old domains. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these benefits persist as model size, dataset size, and context length grow. Our results demonstrate the potential of alternative conditional computation mechanisms for deep neural network architectures. Code and checkpoints are available on GitHub at https://github.com/Ma-Lab-Berkeley/Nestor .

infographic.key_insight: Nestor combines attention-based conditional computation with MoE sparsity, improving language-model pretraining at equal compute and sparsity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Nested sparsity may inform efficient engineering foundation models, but this paper does not demonstrate solid-mechanics or FEM-surrogate applications.
method: Introduce conditional computation that generalizes the transformer attention operator.
Hierarchically compose attention-side sparsity with MoE sparsity.
Evaluate Nestor in language-model pretraining and continual adaptation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports better pretraining performance, more effective long-context adaptation, and more efficient domain adaptation with less forgetting, with benefits persisting as model size, dataset size, and context length increase.
infographic.watch_item: Equal-compute improvements do not establish wall-clock speedups or accuracy on mechanics tasks; both require direct evaluation.
infographic.paper_title: Nested Sparsity for Scalable Pretraining and Continual Learning

title: Relativistic Plasticity
authors: Joshua, Cadogan, Nils Andersson, Ian Hawke, Thomas Celora
abstract: The elastic crust of a neutron star has long been established as a key player in relevant aspects of neutron star physics. However, the state-of-the-art theory of elasticity is restricted to the perturbative domain and does not account for permanent plastic deformations which should be relevant for pulsar glitches, magnetar flares, and the continuous emission of gravitational waves. Plasticity, however, is a historically challenging phenomenon to model - even in the Newtonian regime. This is owed mainly to its dissipative character and the multiscale methods required to consistently reproduce observed phenomena. In this work, we address this first challenge by making use of recent developments in the variational modelling of dissipative fluids to extend the theory of relativistic elasticity to include plastic phenomenology. The resulting theory possesses the same freedoms as the modern Newtonian formalism, while now being compatible with general relativity. The second law of thermodynamics is then used to introduce the yield criterion of plasticity theory in the relativistic setting.

infographic.key_insight: A variational framework extends relativistic elasticity to include dissipative plastic deformation, with a relativistic yield criterion introduced through the second law of thermodynamics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework provides a constitutive foundation for modeling permanent neutron-star crust deformation relevant to pulsar glitches, magnetar flares, and continuous gravitational-wave emission.
method: Adapt variational methods for dissipative fluids to relativistic elastic matter.
Incorporate plastic phenomenology with constitutive freedoms matching modern Newtonian theory.
Use the second law of thermodynamics to introduce a relativistic yield criterion.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a theoretical formulation but no numerical benchmarks, observational validation, or quantitative performance results.
infographic.watch_item: Numerical implementation and multiscale validation remain unestablished in the abstract, which focuses on the dissipative formulation.
infographic.paper_title: Relativistic Plasticity

title: An Arbitrary-Order Augmented Lagrangian Discrete De Rham Scheme for Contact Mechanics with Tresca Friction
authors: Jérôme Droniou, Raman Kumar, Roland Masson
abstract: We design and analyse an arbitrary-order augmented Lagrangian Discrete de Rham polytopal scheme for contact mechanics in fractured media. The fractures are represented as objects of codimension one in the matrix, a linear elastic medium, and a Tresca friction model is adopted when contact between fracture walls occurs. Both the normal Signorini-type/traction constraint and the Tresca friction law are recast as projection identities, and are combined into a single augmented Lagrangian bilinear form. The displacement is discretised by a DDR space of arbitrary polynomial degree $k\ge 0,$ enriched on the fracture faces by bubble degrees of freedom that ensure stability via the existence of a discrete lifting between the Lagrange multiplier space and the discrete jump of the displacement along the fracture. We establish an abstract error estimate yielding optimal order convergence for the displacement and the Lagrange multiplier variables. Extensive numerical experiments confirm the theoretical analysis and demonstrate the practical accuracy and robustness of the scheme.

infographic.key_insight: An arbitrary-order Discrete de Rham scheme combines augmented Lagrangian contact enforcement with fracture-face enrichment to achieve optimal convergence for displacement and contact multipliers.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports accurate simulation of contact and friction between fracture walls in linearly elastic media on polytopal meshes.
method: Recast normal contact constraints and Tresca friction as projection identities in a unified augmented Lagrangian formulation.
Discretise displacement with arbitrary-degree DDR spaces, enriched by fracture-face bubble degrees of freedom.
Establish stability through a discrete lifting and derive an abstract optimal-order error estimate.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports extensive numerical experiments confirming the convergence analysis and demonstrating practical accuracy and robustness, without specifying quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Fracture-face bubble enrichment is essential to the stability argument and adds implementation complexity.
infographic.paper_title: An Arbitrary-Order Augmented Lagrangian Discrete De Rham Scheme for Contact Mechanics with Tresca Friction

title: REDAR: Reinforcement-Driven Adaptive Regularisation for Class Incremental Learning
authors: Akila Ayanthi, Darshana Priyasad, Tharindu Fernando, Sridha Sridharan, Clinton Fookes, Peyman Moghadam
abstract: Regularisation-based class-incremental learning (CIL) methods control the stability-plasticity trade-off through fixed coefficients tuned offline, independently of the continual learning objective and blind to phase-specific variations in data volume, task difficulty, and class similarity. We argue this is a fundamental mismatch and propose REDAR: Reinforcement-Driven Adaptive Regularisation for Class Incremental Learning, which treats regularisation strength selection as a sequential decision problem. At each incremental phase, a lightweight reinforcement learning (RL) agent observes a compact state of current performance metrics and incoming data statistics, and outputs the distillation coefficients for that phase. To respect CIL's constraint on historical data access, the policy is trained entirely on pseudo-CIL tasks constructed from the initial phase, then deployed on the incremental sequence without further adaptation. Experiments on CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet demonstrate that REDAR reduces forgetting and improves forward transfer over fixed and heuristic baselines, and that policies trained on short pseudo-task horizons transfer effectively to longer incremental runs.

infographic.key_insight: REDAR uses reinforcement learning to select phase-specific distillation strengths, replacing fixed regularisation coefficients in class-incremental learning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could help engineering recognition systems learn new classes while retaining prior knowledge, though solid-mechanics applications are not evaluated.
method: Frame regularisation selection as a sequential decision problem.
Use performance metrics and incoming-data statistics to choose each phase’s distillation coefficients.
Train the policy on pseudo-incremental tasks from initial-phase data, then deploy it without further adaptation.
infographic.evidence_signal: On CIFAR-100 and Tiny-ImageNet, the abstract reports reduced forgetting, improved forward transfer over fixed and heuristic baselines, and transfer from short training horizons to longer incremental runs.
infographic.watch_item: A policy trained only on initial-phase pseudo-tasks may face distribution shifts in later phases; robustness beyond the reported image benchmarks remains untested.
infographic.paper_title: REDAR: Reinforcement-Driven Adaptive Regularisation for Class Incremental Learning

title: Hyperreduction accelerates finite element model updating for the discovery of neural materials
authors: Hagen Holthusen, Matthias Knipper, Kevin Linka
abstract: Finite element model updating is among the most general approaches to discover constitutive models from structural experiments: since the displacement field is computed rather than measured, it accommodates arbitrary geometries, boundary conditions, and sparse or noisy data. However, every loss evaluation requires a nonlinear finite element solve per load step, and training neural materials requires many such evaluations. Intrusive model order reduction lowers this cost while retaining boundary conditions and variational structure. How can a reduced model remain accurate while the network weights change at every training step? We combine proper orthogonal decomposition and energy-conserving sampling and weighting with adjoint sensitivities of the reduced model, and adapt both the trial space and the sampled elements along the optimization path. The constitutive law is a polyconvex neural network: a logarithmic normalization term, together with a zero-anchored input convex architecture and a growth term, renders the energy polyconvex, coercive, and non-negative by construction, independent of the trained weights. We demonstrate the approach on two experimental datasets and one synthetic three-dimensional example. For a two-phase specimen, training time decreases from nine hours to 41 minutes compared with a full-order identification, without loss of accuracy. In the three-dimensional example, six modes replace 48 672 degrees of freedom, 116 of 15 625 elements suffice to evaluate the internal forces, and training takes 13 minutes. In all cases, the identified material reproduces the measured reaction force and predicts the displacement field from the force alone. Hyperreduction makes the discovery of neural materials from structural data affordable while retaining the advantages of finite element model updating.

infographic.key_insight: Adaptive hyperreduction accelerates finite element identification of neural constitutive laws while preserving accuracy as network weights evolve.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineers can identify material behavior from structural force data while accommodating arbitrary geometries, boundary conditions, and sparse or noisy measurements.
method: Combine proper orthogonal decomposition with energy-conserving sampling and weighting.
Adapt reduced trial spaces and sampled elements during optimization, using reduced-model adjoint sensitivities.
Use a neural energy architecture that guarantees polyconvexity, coercivity, and non-negativity by construction.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across two experimental datasets and one synthetic 3D example, the method reproduced reaction forces and predicted displacements; two-phase training fell from 9 hours to 41 minutes without loss of accuracy.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy depends on updating the reduced basis and sampled elements as the constitutive network changes during training.
infographic.paper_title: Hyperreduction accelerates finite element model updating for the discovery of neural materials

title: Elastic theory of ideal liquid crystal elastomers
authors: Zumrat Usmanova, Ruobing Bai
abstract: A liquid crystal elastomer (LCE) exhibits a two-way coupling between its mesogen order and network elasticity: the mesogen order sets the undeformed network conformation, and the network deformation reorients the mesogens. This coupling gives rise to large, reversible stimuli-responsive actuation, as well as to soft elasticity, a finite deformation at nearly zero stress. This article reviews the elastic theory of ideal LCEs, bridging single-chain statistics and continuum constitutive models. The "ideal" elastic behavior rests on the assumption of anisotropic Gaussian chains that retain no memory of the crosslinking state, such that rotating the director costs no free energy. The corresponding neo-classical free energy of a monodomain LCE is non-quasi-convex, with a continuous family of stress-free ground states, leading to thermally induced spontaneous deformation and soft elasticity accommodated by coexisting stripe domains. The quasi-convex relaxation of the free energy classifies the behavior of polydomain LCEs into three phases, each with a distinct macroscopic mechanical response depending on the stretch state. The ideal elastic theory can be further extended to incorporate additional behaviors and physical processes, including thermo- and photomechanical coupling, Frank elasticity from director distortion, semi-soft or non-soft behavior arising from network nonideality, and temperature- and rate-dependent viscoelasticity.

infographic.key_insight: Ideal liquid crystal elastomer theory links molecular anisotropy to reversible actuation and soft deformation through a continuous family of stress-free states.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports constitutive modeling of LCE actuators and compliant structures whose mechanical response depends on mesogen orientation and domain rearrangement.
method: Connect anisotropic Gaussian-chain statistics to neo-classical continuum elasticity.
Explain spontaneous deformation and stripe-domain formation through non-quasi-convex free energy.
Use quasi-convex relaxation to classify polydomain responses into three stretch-dependent phases.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes a theoretical review and phase classification, but reports no experimental datasets or quantitative validation.
infographic.watch_item: Ideal softness assumes no memory of the crosslinking state; practical simulations may require nonideality, director-gradient elasticity, and temperature- or rate-dependent effects.
infographic.paper_title: Elastic theory of ideal liquid crystal elastomers

title: Multi-Material Topology Optimization for Targeted Structural Dynamic Vibration Attenuation
authors: Bir Bahadur Chaudhary, Bidhan Pandey, Bin Ouyang, Shiguang Deng
abstract: Resonance-induced excessive vibrations can degrade performance, reduce reliability, and shorten the service life of engineering structures. To reduce the risk of resonance, structural natural frequencies are generally engineered to be shifted away from excitation frequencies. To achieve these frequency shifts, topology optimization provides a systematic approach to tailor structural stiffness and mass as an effective inverse design approach. Multi-material topology optimization exploits the high-dimensional design space of spatially varying material constituents by simultaneously optimizing material selection and spatial distribution over the design domain, offering great flexibility in controlling natural frequencies. This study proposes a multi-material topology optimization that attenuates excessive structural dynamic vibrations in free-vibration scenarios via a novel multivariate weight-based interpolation method. Additionally, to address non-smoothness due to mode switching amid optimization, we employ a bound formulation with an auxiliary scalar design variable to replace the max-min eigenvalue objective with constraints on individual eigenvalues. Furthermore, we study and compare three optimization formulations for multi-material design to attenuate vibrations, including maximizing fundamental eigenfrequency, maximizing the gap between adjacent eigenfrequencies, and excluding frequencies from targeted frequency bands, which are smoothly approximated by a proposed rational polynomial formulation. Numerical examples are presented to demonstrate the effectiveness and applicability of our proposed method.

infographic.key_insight: Multi-material topology optimization tailors structural stiffness and mass to shift natural frequencies away from targeted resonance-prone bands.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Optimizing material selection and spatial distribution offers a route to reduce resonance risk and improve structural reliability.
method: Use multivariate weight-based interpolation to optimize material selection and distribution.
Handle mode switching with an auxiliary scalar variable and individual eigenvalue constraints.
Compare fundamental-frequency maximization, adjacent-frequency gap maximization, and targeted-band exclusion using a smooth rational polynomial approximation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical examples demonstrate the proposed method and compare three frequency-based optimization formulations; the abstract reports no quantitative gains or experimental validation.
infographic.watch_item: Free-vibration frequency placement alone does not establish vibration-amplitude reduction under realistic forcing and damping.
infographic.paper_title: Multi-Material Topology Optimization for Targeted Structural Dynamic Vibration Attenuation

title: Peridynamic Thermo-Mechanical Modeling of Cracking in Tungsten under Fusion-Relevant Heat Fluxes
authors: Rinkle Juneja, Pablo Seleson, Samuel Temple Reeve, Justin Weinmeister, Gary Staebler
abstract: Plasma-facing materials (PFMs) are the primary armor materials in fusion reactors, protecting reactor wall components from extreme heat fluxes, energetic particles, and intense neutron irradiation. These harsh conditions induce thermo-mechanical stresses, irradiation damage, and overall degradation in PFMs. Among these, thermo-mechanical damage induced by extreme heat flux is one of the key factors limiting the lifetime of PFMs. We present a modeling and simulation approach for predicting thermo-mechanical cracking and damage in tungsten, a leading PFM candidate, under fusion-reactor-relevant heat fluxes. Specifically, we study damage induced by cyclic electron beam (e-beam) exposure under different combinations of base temperature and heat flux. We carry out component-scale thermo-mechanical simulations using CabanaPD, a peridynamics fracture mechanics code, informed by experimental data for recrystallized pure tungsten from the JUDITH e-beam facility. The simulations compare well with the experimental classification and enable identification of cracking thresholds across a range of heat fluxes and base temperatures. These predictions can provide detailed insights into the spatial distribution and temporal accumulation of cracks and damage, while offering a pathway for screening candidate PFMs and quantifying their lifespan under fusion-relevant conditions.

infographic.key_insight: Peridynamic thermo-mechanical simulations identify cracking thresholds in tungsten across base temperatures and cyclic heat fluxes relevant to fusion reactors.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Predicting heat-induced cracking can support plasma-facing material screening and component lifetime assessment.
method: Model component-scale thermo-mechanical fracture using CabanaPD.
Simulate cyclic electron-beam exposure at varying base temperatures and heat fluxes.
Track the spatial distribution and temporal accumulation of cracks and damage.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations informed by JUDITH electron-beam data for recrystallized pure tungsten compare well with experimental damage classifications.
infographic.watch_item: Validation described in the abstract covers electron-beam heating, not combined neutron irradiation and plasma exposure.
infographic.paper_title: Peridynamic Thermo-Mechanical Modeling of Cracking in Tungsten under Fusion-Relevant Heat Fluxes

title: WiMoT: Replay-Free Continual Wi-Fi Sensing via Moment Transport
authors: Chunchun Yang, Yang Cao, Zhitang Chen
abstract: Continual Wi-Fi sensing must balance plasticity, learning new rooms or users, against stability, keeping earlier ones, yet nodes often cannot retain channel state information (CSI) for privacy and storage reasons. We propose WiMoT (Wi-Fi Moment Transport), which stores the per-class feature mean and covariance of every earlier domain instead of samples. When the representation changes, stored statistics become stale. WiMoT restricts the change to an affine map on a frozen feature basis and applies the same map to the statistics, so they stay valid without old samples. Supervised contrastive learning learns the new domain, a closed-form loss on the stored statistics keeps earlier classes separable, and a Gaussian discriminant classifier, refitted from the transported statistics with equal weight per domain, predicts without domain identity. On 3DO, WiMANS, and Widar3.0, WiMoT's average final accuracies are 94.02%, 89.61%, and 95.16% with at most 0.58 percentage points (pp) of forgetting. On 3DO and Widar3.0, it also has the highest balance of new- and earlier-domain accuracy and is 3.77 and 13.11 pp ahead of the strongest of 21 baselines, which uses replay, staying ahead across domain orders and label budgets. On WiMANS, it matches the strongest replay baseline in accuracy (+0.41 pp) while reducing forgetting from 2.78 to 0.00 pp, and has the highest six-order average accuracy. Because full covariances dominate the memory, storing them as rank-32 factors shrinks the moment memory to 6.4%, losing at most 0.49 pp of accuracy, within edge-node storage budgets.

infographic.key_insight: WiMoT enables replay-free continual Wi-Fi sensing by transporting stored class means and covariances through an affine feature update instead of retaining earlier CSI samples.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For privacy- and storage-constrained wireless sensing nodes—not solid-mechanics constitutive models—WiMoT supports learning new rooms or users while preserving earlier-domain accuracy.
method: Store per-class feature means and covariances for each earlier domain.
Learn an affine update on a frozen feature basis, transporting stored moments while balancing new-domain learning and earlier-class separation.
Refit a Gaussian discriminant classifier with equal domain weighting; predict without domain identity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 3DO, WiMANS, and Widar3.0, reported final accuracies are 94.02%, 89.61%, and 95.16%, with at most 0.58 percentage points of forgetting; rank-32 covariance storage uses 6.4% of full moment memory with at most 0.49 points of accuracy loss.
infographic.watch_item: Restricting representation changes to an affine map on a frozen basis may limit adaptation to shifts beyond those evaluated.
infographic.paper_title: WiMoT: Replay-Free Continual Wi-Fi Sensing via Moment Transport

title: DRIVE: Fine-tuning via Data Contribution- and Diversity-aware Weighting with Prior Regularization
authors: Qing Liu, Xinrui Chen, Yi Du, Ou Wu, Weiyao Zhu
abstract: Single-stage fine-tuning is pervasive, yet catastrophic forgetting persists when the source pre-training data is inaccessible. Data weighting affords a natural lever to modulate sample influence. Yet existing weighting methods lack a principled mechanism to explicitly arbitrate knowledge retention against new-task adaptation, and provide no unified differentiable objective to accommodate auxiliary signals such as sample diversity and sample characteristics. This is because current schemes privilege one goal over the other, and no explicit gradient-compatible encoding exists for such signals. To address this, we propose DRIVE, a principled and efficient weight assignment framework. It derives per-sample weights via a unified differentiable objective where three coupled signals co-evolve: Shapley additivity splits contribution into anti-forgetting and adaptation components, which are reshaped by a covariance-based diversity term and stabilized by a sample-characteristic prior. Far from a mere combination, this yields an end-to-end gradient-based scheme balancing stability against plasticity. Theoretically, we prove that DRIVE enjoys superior stability-plasticity guarantees over existing weighting schemes and enhances parameter estimation robustness. Empirically, it attains superior overall performance, faster convergence, and stronger robustness. Code at https://github.com/luciabcd/DRIVE.

infographic.key_insight: DRIVE learns per-sample fine-tuning weights that balance retaining pretrained knowledge with adapting to a new task.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For mechanics-oriented AI models, DRIVE could help adapt pretrained models to new datasets when original training data is unavailable, though the abstract reports no solid-mechanics validation.
method: Decompose sample contributions into anti-forgetting and adaptation components using Shapley additivity.
Modulate contributions with covariance-based diversity and regularize weights using sample-characteristic priors.
Optimize weights through a unified differentiable objective.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical stability–plasticity and estimation-robustness guarantees, plus empirical gains in overall performance, convergence speed, and robustness, without naming datasets or giving numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Assess contribution-estimation cost and sensitivity to prior choices before applying DRIVE to mechanics datasets.
infographic.paper_title: DRIVE: Fine-tuning via Data Contribution- and Diversity-aware Weighting with Prior Regularization

title: A high-order multi-scale method and its error analysis for nonlocal-in-time fractionally damped wave problems in composite materials
authors: Gehao Wang, Hao Dong, Yufeng Nie, Junzhi Cui
abstract: Significant spatial heterogeneity and nonlocal history-dependent attenuation jointly govern wave propagation in composite materials, making full-scale direct numerical simulation (DNS) computationally prohibitive. This study proposed a high-order multi-scale (HOMS) method for nonlocal-in-time fractionally damped wave problems with highly oscillatory and discontinuous material coefficients. Using a multi-scale asymptotic expansion approach, the macroscopic homogenized equation, and first- and second-order correction terms are derived to construct the high-accuracy HOMS solution. Moreover, a local pointwise error analysis identifies the leading residual eliminated by this HOMS solution and validates its local physical balance preservation. Then, a global energy-norm error estimate establishes the $O(\varepsilon)$-order convergence rate for the HOMS solution. Subsequently, an efficient spatiotemporal multi-scale algorithm integrating the finite element and finite difference methods is designed, which employs a novel fully discrete $L2\text{-}1_σ$-Newmark scheme, and corresponding unconditional shifted-energy stability and explicit convergence rates are also obtained for the macroscopic homogenized displacement and velocity, respectively. Both two- and three-dimensional examples are presented to demonstrate the accuracy, efficiency, reduced cost, and robustness of the proposed HOMS method. This work provides an effective multi-scale tool for nonlocal-in-time wave simulation in engineering applications.

infographic.key_insight: A high-order multiscale method captures heterogeneous wave propagation with fractional history-dependent damping using homogenized dynamics and first- and second-order corrections.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method reduces the computational burden of simulating waves in composite materials with rapidly varying, discontinuous properties.
method: Derive a homogenized wave equation and microscale corrections through multiscale asymptotic expansion.
Establish local balance preservation and global O(ε) energy-norm convergence.
Combine finite elements with an L2-1σ–Newmark time scheme and prove unconditional shifted-energy stability.
infographic.evidence_signal: Two- and three-dimensional numerical examples demonstrate accuracy, efficiency, reduced computational cost, and robustness, although the abstract reports no quantitative speedups.
infographic.watch_item: Implementation must account for fractional-history storage and computation, which the abstract does not quantify.
infographic.paper_title: A high-order multi-scale method and its error analysis for nonlocal-in-time fractionally damped wave problems in composite materials

title: A linear dual-field finite element method for incompressible MHD, part I: cross-helicity and Alfvénic alignment in periodic domains
authors: Shusheng Li, Siyuan Tong, Qilong Zhai, Qian Zhang
abstract: Cross helicity, together with total energy, determines the Elsässer energies and thus quantifies departures from Alfvénic alignment in incompressible MHD. Building on the dual-field method in [Mao and Xi, \emph{J. Comput. Phys.}, 2025], we construct a linear finite element method for periodic domains that reproduces the cross-helicity balance. We connect the discrete energy and cross-helicity conservation laws to Alfvénic alignment through a nonnegative Elsässer-energy representation, establishing preservation of the corresponding exact relation when either Elsässer energy is initially zero in the unforced ideal case. We reassign the two discrete approximations of the magnetic field to the integer and half-integer time levels and redesign the Lorentz and induction couplings within the Mao-Xi formulation. The resulting scheme uses linear staggered updates and retains the energy balances, strong and weak divergence-free properties, and magnetic- and fluid-helicity balances. Numerical experiments illustrate the role of the cross-helicity balance in preserving an aligned state in the ideal case and in alignment dynamics under weak dissipation.

infographic.key_insight: A linear dual-field finite element scheme reproduces cross-helicity balance and preserves exact Alfvénic alignment in unforced ideal incompressible MHD when either Elsässer energy is initially zero.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Preserving alignment and conservation laws supports physically consistent simulations of conducting-fluid flows in periodic domains.
method: Reassign the two magnetic-field approximations to integer and half-integer time levels.
Redesign Lorentz and induction couplings within linear staggered updates.
Link energy and cross-helicity balances to a nonnegative Elsässer-energy representation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments illustrate aligned-state preservation in ideal MHD and alignment dynamics under weak dissipation; the abstract reports no quantitative accuracy or runtime results.
infographic.watch_item: The formulation targets periodic domains, so applicability to engineering boundary conditions requires further assessment.
infographic.paper_title: A linear dual-field finite element method for incompressible MHD, part I: cross-helicity and Alfvénic alignment in periodic domains

title: Conservative Finite Element Methods for Kirchhoff-Type Equations
authors: Benjamin Dörich, Felix Krumbiegel, Jemal Rogava, Andreas Rupp, Zurab Vashakidze
abstract: We construct and analyse a fully discrete scheme for a Kirchhoff-type nonlinear integro-differential equation in two spatial dimensions with time-dependent coefficients. The scheme combines a symmetric three-layer time discretization of Crank--Nicolson type with a conforming finite element method of arbitrary polynomial degree $p$ and a Picard iteration for the nonlinearity. We prove that the Picard iteration is well defined and, that the iterates converge to the Ritz projection of the exact solution measured in fractional-power norms of the discrete Laplacian. Running the same energy argument in the unshifted norms, and under the same hypotheses, we then obtain the optimal order $\mathcal{O} ( h^{p+1} + τ^2 )$ in $L^2$ and $\mathcal{O} ( h^{p} + τ^2 )$ in $H^1$ for the full error. For the homogeneous problem with constant coefficients, the exact solution of the scheme moreover preserves a discrete energy identically. Numerical experiments with manufactured solutions reproduce the predicted second order in time and the full spatial order $h^{p+1}$ in the $L^2$-norm.

infographic.key_insight: A fully discrete finite element scheme for Kirchhoff-type equations achieves optimal spatial accuracy and second-order time accuracy while exactly preserving discrete energy for homogeneous, constant-coefficient problems.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports accurate simulation of nonlinear, nonlocal dynamics relevant to structural mechanics, with energy conservation in a restricted setting.
method: Conforming finite elements of arbitrary polynomial degree p in two spatial dimensions.
Symmetric three-layer, Crank–Nicolson-type time discretization.
Picard iteration for the nonlinearity, supported by convergence and error analysis.
infographic.evidence_signal: Manufactured-solution experiments reproduce second-order temporal convergence and the predicted h^(p+1) spatial convergence in L².
infographic.watch_item: Exact discrete-energy preservation is established only for the homogeneous, constant-coefficient case; convergence and error guarantees depend on the analysis hypotheses.
infographic.paper_title: Conservative Finite Element Methods for Kirchhoff-Type Equations

title: Can Language Models Get "Aphasia" From Neuronal Ablation?
authors: Pratik Worah, Randall Bateman
abstract: Progressive neuronal loss is the hallmark of neurodegenerative disease, yet how loss of neurons shapes the pattern of cognitive decline remains poorly understood. Here we systematically ablate neurons (computational units) in language models spanning recurrent long short-term memory (LSTM) and Transformer architectures and apply limited fine-tuning as a simple proxy for compensatory plasticity. With whole-unit ablation, LSTMs degrade gradually with syntactic and semantic faculties declining in parallel across mild-to-moderate damage. By contrast, Transformers exhibit late threshold-like collapse under feedforward multi-layer perceptron (MLP) ablation and smoother sigmoid-like decline under attention-head ablation. Qualitatively, MLP-ablated models continue to make within-category semantic substitutions (semantic paraphasias) alongside rising non-responses, paralleling Wernicke-type aphasia, while attention-head ablation produces a trend toward loss of semantic specificity similar to the semantic variant of primary progressive aphasia (svPPA). These findings indicate that feedforward and attentional pathways have functionally distinct failure modes, suggesting that architecture-dependent failure profiles may offer new computational perspectives on aphasic syndromes and neurodegenerative diseases as an in silico model. Notably, early accuracy retention under Transformer attention-head ablation qualitatively parallels pre-symptomatic reserve before the 40--60% neuronal loss reported by Gomez-Isla et al. (1996) when clinical symptoms emerge in Alzheimer's disease, whereas the steadier LSTM decline parallels the symptomatic progression described by DeKosky and Scheff (1990) and Terry et al. (1991).

infographic.key_insight: Simulated neuronal damage produces architecture-dependent language failures: gradual decline in LSTMs, late collapse under Transformer MLP ablation, and smoother decline under attention-head ablation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These failure profiles offer a computational analogy for progressive damage and functional reserve, rather than a validated solid-mechanics damage model.
method: Systematically ablate computational units in LSTM and Transformer language models.
Compare Transformer feedforward MLP and attention-head ablation.
Apply limited fine-tuning as a proxy for compensatory plasticity.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports parallel syntactic and semantic decline in LSTMs, versus distinct Transformer degradation curves and qualitative semantic errors resembling aspects of aphasia.
infographic.watch_item: Aphasia and neurodegeneration parallels are qualitative; computational ablation and limited fine-tuning do not establish biological equivalence.
infographic.paper_title: Can Language Models Get "Aphasia" From Neuronal Ablation?
